card.h1: The Module, the Rule, the Model: Visual Transformation Across Three Media Regimes
Every media revolution moves the designer one step further from the artifact

ul.li: European printers industrialized the module: a letter cast once, reused everywhere, at a scale that reorganized the book trade
Swiss modernism and desktop publishing turned layout into a rule that generates pages the designer never draws
Generative systems make the deliverable a model: we specify intent and judge output we did not compose
The claim to test today: each shift traded direct control for reach, and each time the discipline argued about what was lost

card.h1: Five dates that reorganized the discipline

ul.li: 1455 — Mainz: metal type scales into an industry. Printing itself is much older; this date marks European adoption, not origin
1928 — Tschichold's Die neue Typographie: the page becomes a system
1964 — Gerstner's Designing Programmes: the design becomes a program
1985 — PageMaker: the print trades collapse into one desk
2016 — Variable fonts: type becomes a continuous space

card.h1: I. European metal type: the letter as a manufactured part
Mainz industrialized the module; it did not invent it

ul.li: The earliest dated printed book is Chinese: a woodblock Diamond Sutra scroll from Dunhuang, its colophon dated 11 May 868
Bi Sheng cut individual baked-clay characters between 1041 and 1048, recorded by Shen Kuo; cast-metal type was in use in Korea from the 13th century
The Jikji, printed with movable metal type at Heungdeoksa in July 1377, is the oldest surviving metal-type book, 78 years before the 42-line Bible
So Gutenberg's achievement is specific: cast metal sorts, oily ink and the press combined into a workshop that could run a large edition in Europe
Interpretation: what spread from Mainz was industrial adoption, and the visual consequences we study follow from that scale

card.h1: The 42-line Bible was a factory imitating a scriptorium

ul.li: Production is the story: roughly 16,000 pieces of type, nearly 50,000 sheets of paper, about three years of work
Around 180 copies, some 45 on parchment rather than paper
Scholars read a mid-production decision to enlarge the run from pages set twice, an increase estimated near 30%
Visually it imitated German manuscript hands, down to the dense black textura and hand-finished initials
Teaching point: a new medium's first masterpiece is usually a facsimile of the thing it displaces

card.h1: The page became an interface

ul.li: Type-set editions made near-identical copies at volume, and identical copies made reference possible
Title page, page numbers, running heads, indexes, tables of contents, footnotes: navigational furniture that settled into a standard kit in European printed books across the century after 1455

Elizabeth Eisenstein called this typographic fixity. Her argument, and it is an argument rather than a measurement, is that a text which stays put can be cited, corrected and disputed across cities and generations
Design consequence: standardization is not the enemy of thought, it is the precondition for comparison

card.h1: The grid: a moral argument disguised as a layout tool

ul.li: Tschichold, 1928: asymmetry, sans serif and the flush-left rag as an ethical position against ornament and nationalism
Müller-Brockmann, Grid Systems, 1981: the grid as a means of introducing order, the designer as neutral servant of the message
The claim was objectivity: identical rules applied to any content yield clarity independent of taste
The critique, then and now: neutrality is itself a style, and a Swiss grid is a mid-century European aesthetic rather than a law of perception
Note the structural change. The designer now authors a system and delegates the individual page to it

card.h1: Gerstner, 1964: designing programmes, before the tools existed

ul.li: Karl Gerstner proposed systematic design as a model, across four essays, explicitly at the dawn of the computer era
His move: stop designing the solution, design the set of all acceptable solutions, then select from it
A parameter-driven identity or a modular typeface is not a layout, it is a description of a space of layouts
Lars Müller reissued the book because the argument now reads as a specification for computational design
The lecture's hinge: programmatic design is a design idea that computers later industrialized, not a consequence of them

card.h1: II. The digital era: the rule becomes executable
1985: three products collapse five centuries of trades

ul.li: Paul Brainerd described the shift as a three-legged stool: the Macintosh of 1984, Adobe PostScript, and Aldus PageMaker, released July 1985
He coined desktop publishing to market it; the term named an industry that did not yet exist
PostScript mattered most: a page described as code, resolution-independent, printable anywhere
Compositor, typesetter, paste-up artist and platemaker became one person at one desk. Enormous access, real deskilling
Aldus named itself after Aldus Manutius, the Venetian printer. The new medium reached for old legitimacy

card.h1: Emigre: designing with the machine's grain

ul.li: Early screens and printers offered coarse pixel grids, and much of the profession read this as degradation of the typographic tradition
Zuzana Licko drew bitmap faces that took the pixel as the module rather than hiding it. The constraint became the design language
Her line, you read best what you read most, attacked the claim that legibility is a fixed property of forms rather than a habit of readers
Emigre magazine turned that argument into a decade-long public quarrel about authorship and taste
Transferable method: when a new medium looks ugly, ask whether you are seeing a defect or an unfamiliar grain

card.h1: 2010: the page dissolves, and layout becomes a rule you cannot preview

ul.li: Ethan Marcotte published Responsive Web Design in A List Apart on 25 May 2010, after naming the idea in a talk that April
Three ingredients, nothing more: fluid grids, flexible images, media queries
He built on John Allsopp's argument that print's control is simply a function of the limitation of the printed page
The artifact stops being a composition and becomes a set of relationships that resolve differently on every device
Fixity is now optional. What you approve is a behaviour, not an image

card.h1: 2016: type stops being a set of objects and becomes a space

ul.li: Apple, Google, Microsoft and Adobe announced variable fonts at ATypI Warsaw on 14 September 2016, as OpenType 1.8
John Hudson's definition: a single font file that behaves like multiple fonts
Up to 64,000 axes of variation are permitted, and named instances such as Bold are coordinates the designer chose to label
The interpolation is authored, not automatic stretching. The type designer defines how each axis behaves
This is Gerstner's programme shipped as a file format: you deliver the space, the context picks the instance

card.h1: III. Computational intelligence: the model becomes the medium
What actually changed: the specification stopped being explicit

ul.li: A grid, a stylesheet and a variable font are deterministic systems. You can read the rule and predict the output
A generative model is a statistical system fitted to prior images and text. Its rule is not inspectable, and the same input need not repeat
So the designer's input moves again: from drawing, to ruling, to prompting, curating and rejecting
The scarce skill inverts. Production capacity becomes nearly free, and judgment about which output is right becomes the bottleneck
Honest framing: this is a shift in the cost structure of making, not evidence that taste has been automated

card.h1: The new failure mode is plausibility, not error

ul.li: A model trained on the corpus of existing design reproduces its centre of gravity: competent, familiar, averaged, and recognizable as such
Print's failure mode was a mistake you could point to. This one is work that is merely unremarkable, which is harder to argue against in a meeting
Three open problems you will be paid to have opinions about: provenance of training data, homogenization of visual culture, and accountability for output nobody composed
The counter-move is not refusal but specificity: brief against the average, bring material the corpus does not contain, and edit hard

card.h1: Three regimes, one direction of travel

ul.li: Read the bottom row across: every revolution has relocated scarcity, never abolished it
The regime dates are European and industrial markers for this lecture's argument, not claims about where each technique first appeared

card.h1: Muriel Cooper designed the transition itself, in the 1970s

ul.li: Cooper, 1925 to 1994, spent four decades at MIT: the first designer in its Office of Publications, then design director of the MIT Press
She co-founded the Visible Language Workshop in the mid-1970s and became founding faculty of the Media Lab
Her consistent concern across print and screen: tools and interfaces giving designers greater control and quicker feedback, eventually aided by machine intelligence
Her Information Landscapes treated typography as something that moves, scales and responds, presented the year she died
Why she closes the argument: she established metaphors and trained designers who shaped the digital landscape we inherit

card.h1: What remains your job

ul.li: Five centuries of this history have automated execution repeatedly and decision never
Each transition rewarded the designers who learned the new medium's grain instead of defending the previous medium's finish
Take with you: know what your system generates, know what it cannot, and be able to say why this output and not the plausible one beside it

Seminar question: the 42-line Bible imitated the manuscript, the first web pages imitated the printed page, and generated images imitate photography and illustration. What is the native form of a computational medium, and who decides?

brief.instruction: Academic but spoken — a confident lecturer who argues rather than surveys. Plain declarative sentences; specialist terms (module, fixity, interpolation, statistical prior) used precisely and glossed once in plain language. About 55 words per slide, bulleted; the template holds median 66 words, p90 117, so budget 55–65 a slide and go toward 100 only on a deliberately dense slide such as the comparison table card, the priority-qualification card, or a chapter argument. Audience: undergraduate visual communication design students. They know Helvetica, Bauhaus, and InDesign; they do not know Eisenstein, Gerstner, or PostScript. Assume visual literacy, not historical or technical literacy — every proper name gets one clause saying who or what it is, every date earns its place by marking a change in practice. Vary sentence and paragraph length. Never the "Bold term: explanation" list format for a whole slide. No signposting phrases ("Let's explore", "In this section"). No sweeping openers or inspirational closers — start and end on substance. None of the "not just X — it's Y" contrast family. No em dashes. Keep every figure, date, name and quotation exactly as written in the outline; these are researched and cited. Do not add statistics, dates, or attributed quotations that are not in the outline. Where the outline hedges ("roughly", "estimated near", "near-identical"), keep the hedge.

This lecture makes historical claims to design students, so the register of each claim must stay visible in the writing. Facts: dated, cited events and quantities. Reproduce them as written, with their citations, and never round or sharpen a hedged figure. Interpretation: named scholarly or curatorial arguments, such as Eisenstein on typographic fixity, the critique of Swiss neutrality, and this lecture's own module/rule/model thesis. Attribute them to whoever argues them, or mark them as the lecture's reading. Do not restate an interpretation as a measured finding. Illustrative assumptions: the three regimes and their date ranges are a teaching frame for European and industrial practice, not a periodization of world media history. Where the frame is used, say that it is a frame. Priority language is the specific risk to avoid. Do not write that Gutenberg invented movable type, reusable letter modules, or printing, and do not call the 42-line Bible the first printed book. Printing with reusable type is older and East Asian in origin, as the outline's cited 868, 1041–48, 13th-century and 1377 items establish. Any superlative that survives must be exactly as narrow as its source: "earliest dated printed book", "oldest surviving movable metal type book", "Europe's first large edition from cast metal type". The East Asian material is one qualifying slide plus one timeline clause and stays that size; it corrects the claim without becoming a second lecture.

Editorial and grid-driven, in the template's textbook register: white paper, one structural ink, hairline rules, ruled figure boxes with numbered captions beneath, generous margins. Rational and restrained throughout. Density must vary deliberately: the three chapter dividers are near-empty type-only act breaks, the comparison table and the timeline are dense and structural, and the argument slides sit between them. Imagery is selected and historical, never decorative stock, and roughly half the content slides should carry a visual. Priorities for figures: the Dunhuang Diamond Sutra scroll and East Asian type sorts on the qualification slide; a 42-line Bible page and European metal type sorts; early print navigational furniture (title page, index, running head); a Swiss grid diagram; the 1984 Macintosh with the LaserWriter; a coarse bitmap alphabet; a responsive layout reflowing across three widths; a variable font axis diagram; Cooper's Information Landscapes. Where a real archival image is not available, prefer a thin-line technical figure or a typographic diagram over a generic illustration, and let a slide stay purely typographic rather than filling it. Captions carry the qualification where the picture could mislead: a type-sorts figure is captioned by its own tradition and date, never as the origin of type. Build the slides that argue structurally: the five-date timeline as the native horizontal timeline band; the three-regimes slide as the ruled record table from the attached data; the 1985 three-legged stool and the responsive-design triad as diagrams of three parts rather than bullet lists; the variable-font slide as an axis or interpolation diagram. Captions stay native text below the figure, never inside the image. No charts unless the data is supplied here. Every attachment-list in this outline is the final element of its card, after the textual content, and must stay there. The recurring motif worth holding across the deck: the module, the grid line, and the parameter axis are the same idea at three scales, so repeat the hairline grid as the deck's visual argument.
